name: Complementary Colors
statement: Opposite each other on the colour wheel, complements cancel to grey and, side by side, intensify.
statementAccent: complements cancel to grey and, side by side, intensify
meaning: Complementary colours are pairs of colours that lie opposite each other on a colour wheel and that, when combined or mixed in the right proportions, cancel each other out to produce a neutral grey, white, or black. Which colours count as complementary depends on the colour model in use, because the additive model of light, the subtractive model of pigments, and the traditional artists' model give different pairs. In the additive light model, the complementary pairs are red and cyan, green and magenta, and blue and yellow, and mixing each pair of lights produces white. In the traditional artists' model based on red, yellow, and blue, the familiar complements are red and green, blue and orange, and yellow and purple. Complementary colours have a distinctive perceptual relationship: staring at a colour produces an afterimage in its complement, and placing two complements side by side makes each appear more vivid, a high-contrast effect that artists and designers exploit deliberately.
mechanism: Complementary colours are defined by cancellation. In the additive model, two complementary lights together contain the full range of the spectrum, so mixing them at full intensity yields white; this is why red and cyan, green and magenta, and blue and yellow are the additive complements. In pigment and traditional models, mixing complements combines colorants that between them absorb across the spectrum, tending toward a neutral dark. Beyond mixing, complements are linked in perception through the opponent-process organization of colour vision, in which colours are coded in antagonistic channels. This is why afterimages appear in the complement: staring at a colour fatigues one side of an opponent channel, so on looking at a neutral surface the opposite side dominates and the complement is seen. The same opponent coding underlies simultaneous contrast, in which a colour placed against its complement, or on a coloured background, has its appearance pushed toward the complement of the surround, making adjacent complements look more saturated and vibrant. Which specific pairs are complementary shifts with the colour model, since additive light and traditional pigment wheels place different colours opposite one another.

examples.text: In the light model, red and cyan, green and magenta, and blue and yellow are complements, each pair mixing to white.
On the traditional red-yellow-blue wheel, red and green, blue and orange, and yellow and purple are the familiar complementary pairs.
Placed next to each other, complementary colours make each other appear brighter and more intense, a contrast artists use deliberately.

variants.name: Model dependence
variants.text: The fact that which colours are complementary depends on the colour model, so additive light and traditional pigment wheels give different pairs.

variants.name: The afterimage link
variants.text: The appearance of a colour's complement in the negative afterimage, arising from opponent-process colour coding.

whyItMatters: Complementary colours are a central concept in colour theory, art, and design, describing the pairs of colours with the strongest visual relationship. Placed side by side, complements create maximum contrast and appear to intensify one another, a powerful tool that painters from the Impressionists onward, and modern designers, use to make colours vivid, to draw attention, and to create striking harmonies or tensions. Mixed together, complements neutralise each other, which artists exploit to dull or grey a colour and to mix natural-looking shadows. The concept also connects to the science of vision: the afterimages seen in complementary colours and the shifts of simultaneous contrast both arise from the opponent-process coding of colour, so complements reveal something about how the eye and brain process colour. Because the complementary pairs depend on the colour model, the concept also clarifies the difference between mixing light and mixing pigment.

working.text: locate the colour directly across the colour wheel of the model in use.
combine the pair to produce a neutral grey, white, or black, since together they span the spectrum or absorb across it.
place the complements side by side to make each appear brighter and more saturated through contrast.

limits: Which colours are complementary depends entirely on the colour model, so the additive light pairs, such as red and cyan, differ from the traditional artists' pairs, such as red and green, and stating a complement without naming the model is ambiguous. The cancellation to a neutral holds in principle and in the right proportions, but real pigments are imperfect, so mixing artists' complements often yields a muddy brown rather than a pure grey. The perceptual effects, afterimages and the intensification of adjacent complements, arise from opponent-process vision and are matters of perception rather than physics alone.
misreadings: Complementary colours are not a single fixed set; the pairs depend on the colour model, so red's complement is cyan in the light model but green on the traditional artists' wheel. Mixing complements does not brighten a colour but neutralises it toward grey, while placing them side by side intensifies them, so mixing and juxtaposing have opposite effects. And the afterimage in a complement is a perceptual effect of opponent-process vision, not a property of the pigment, so treating complements as one universal pair, expecting mixing to brighten, or the afterimage as physical, misreads a model-dependent relationship of colours that cancel and contrast.
origin: A foundational concept in colour theory: pairs of colours opposite on the colour wheel that cancel to neutral when mixed and intensify when juxtaposed, with pairs depending on the colour model and effects linked to opponent-process vision.
